\subsection{Models undercount repetitions, proportionally}

Figure~\ref{fig:main}(a) shows the relative count error against $k$. Below
$k\!=\!6$ every model is essentially exact; from $k\!=\!6$ the panel splits.
Pooled at $k\ge6$, repeated items are rendered with a median error of
\ErrRep{}\% $[\ErrRepLo{}, \ErrRepHi{}]$ ($n=\ErrRepN{}$), one-directional:
models produce \emph{fewer} repetitions than requested, never systematically
more.

Within $k\le32$, though, the deficit is \emph{proportional}, not saturating ---
not what Theorem~\ref{thm:collapse}(iv) predicts. A constant fits the panel's
median count above $k\!=\!6$ with residual sum of squares \ShapeSatSSE{} against
\ShapePropSSE{} for $\hat c=\ShapePropSlope{}k$, in \ShapePropModels{} of
\ErrNModels{} checkpoints (S10). A finite $N^\ast$ implies the count levels off;
here it tracks the request, so the horizon is not inside this ladder.

\subsection{Past the ladder, the count does level off}

So we extended it, post hoc, to $k\in\{48,64,96,128\}$ on \HzModelNames{} --- the
checkpoints whose decoders admit utterances that long (S10). Tracking stops: the
repeated median \emph{falls} from \HzMedRepKLo{} at $k\!=\!48$ to \HzMedRepKHi{}
at $k\!=\!128$ as the request grows threefold. Of \HzNGen{} generations
\HzExclCap{} hit our budget and \HzExclDegen{} were degenerate, leaving
\HzNCellLo{}--\HzNCellHi{} per cell; dropping truncated items is conservative,
since their counts are censored downward and keeping them would deepen the
apparent saturation.

The controls stop us reading this as counting collapse alone: they saturate too,
near \HzMedCtlKHi{} units, so these decoders have a general utterance-length
ceiling and the reportable quantity is the \emph{ratio}, which divides it out.
Fitting the descriptive form $\hat c(k)=\hat K(1-e^{-k/\hat K})$ over the combined
ladder --- $\hat K$ is a saturation scale read off counts, \emph{not} the
theorem's $N^\ast$, which is a function of the unmeasured $q$ --- gives
$\hat K_{\mathrm{rep}}=\HzNRep{}$ $[\HzNRepLo{},\HzNRepHi{}]$ against
$\hat K_{\mathrm{ctl}}=\HzNCtl{}$ $[\HzNCtlLo{},\HzNCtlHi{}]$, bootstrapped over
items and disjoint in \HzNSep{} of \HzNModels{}: repetition lowers the counting
horizon \HzRatio{}-fold. The theorem predicts saturation of this kind just past
where our original ladder stopped, which is why $k\le32$ looked proportional.

Two things keep this short of clean confirmation: the panel is \HzNModels{}
checkpoints, and a pure horizon predicts a plateau whereas the repeated median
\emph{declines} (\HzDeclinePeak{}$\rightarrow$\HzDeclineLast{}). The judge's bias
points the same way (S9), making \HzRatio{} an upper bound.

What degrades with $k$ is reliability rather than proportion: the share rendered
\emph{exactly} right falls from \ExactRepKLo{}\% at $k\!=\!\ExactRepKLoVal{}$ to
\ExactRepKHi{}\% at $k\!=\!\ExactRepKHiVal{}$, and holds for word, sentence and
place-value units alike.

Because the claim is about models, not about our corpus, we take the checkpoint
as the unit of replication, reducing each to its own repeated-minus-control
difference. The exactly-correct rate favours the control in all \CkExactN{} (mean
\CkExact{} points $[\CkExactLo{},\CkExactHi{}]$, signed-rank $p=\CkExactP{}$,
the exact floor at $n\!=\!6$). The median-error gap is positive in \CkErrNPos{}
of \CkErrN{} and zero in \ErrBestModel{}, so $p=\CkErrP{}$: on that statistic the
panel misses even its own floor, which we report rather than counting votes.

\subsection{The limit is periodicity, not length}

Figure~\ref{fig:main}(b) is the paper's sharpest test. Each control has its
twin's carrier and word count, differing only in that the $k$ copies of one word
become non-adjacent ones. Were the failure about length, attention span or
exposure bias, the curves would coincide. They do not: at $k\ge6$ the median
control error is \ErrCtl{}\% $[\ErrCtlLo{}, \ErrCtlHi{}]$ over $n=\ErrCtlN{}$
generations, at every $k$ up to $32$, for every model. The contrast is sharpest
in exactly-correct renderings --- \ExactCtl{}\% for controls against
\ExactRep{}\% for their twins: decoders that miscount a repeated sequence five
times in six render its non-adjacent twin correctly nineteen times in twenty. Controls are not perfect --- the residual \CtlMissPct{}\% carry
genuine truncations --- but they are exact where the repeated items are not.

Two rivals --- that repeated text is simply improbable, and that the attractor is
acoustic --- fail their own predictions (S8).

\subsection{The decoder buys states more slowly under repetition}

Theorem~\ref{thm:collapse}(ii) says states visited under periodic conditioning
stop being mutually distinguishable, so more repetitions should buy distinct
internal states more slowly than non-repetitive text of the same length does. We
count states by the effective rank $\mathcal{N}_{\mathrm{eff}} = \exp(-\sum_i p_i
\log p_i)$ of the trajectory over normalised singular values, and report the
\emph{capacity gain} $\mathrm{d}\mathcal{N}_{\mathrm{eff}}/\mathrm{d}\log k$.

Figure~\ref{fig:main}(c,d) shows the result. On repeated text the capacity gain
is a factor \CapRatio{} of the control gain; the gap is positive in all
\CkCapN{} checkpoints (mean \CkCap{} $[\CkCapLo{},\CkCapHi{}]$, $p=\CkCapP{}$)
but varies fourfold across them (SD \CkCapSD{}), so the mechanism is general in
direction, not in magnitude.

An obvious objection is circularity: rendering \emph{very} sixteen times really
does produce monotonous audio, so a low-rank trajectory might follow from the
stimulus rather than lost capacity. It does not. Adding realised output diversity
(type/token ratio, adjacent-repeat rate, length) as covariates leaves the ratio
at \CapAdjRatio{}, and restricting to correctly rendered items leaves it at
\CapCorrRatio{} --- though that filter keeps \ExactCtl{}\% of controls against
\ExactRep{}\% of repeated items, so it is not like-for-like. The gain stays
\emph{positive} in \CapPosModels{} of \ErrNModels{}: at $k\le32$ repetition
slows state acquisition without halting it.

Lemma~\ref{lem:dilution}'s premise holds only approximately: renormalised over
the $k$ repeated key columns, the most-attended occurrence takes
$\ShareMaxK{}/k$ of the block's mass at worst, so $\delta\le\DeltaMax{}$ nats
(S4). It holds in
aggregate only, and we should not claim more: \emph{within} a $(\text{model},k)$
cell, where $k$ is fixed, items with flatter attention are counted
\emph{better}, not worse ($r=\DilR{}$ $[\DilRLo{},\DilRHi{}]$ over \DilCells{}
cells, all \DilNAgainst{} measures agreeing; controls give $\DilCtlR{}$
$[\DilCtlLo{},\DilCtlHi{}]$). That reverses the lemma's direction, so dilution
does not select which generations fail --- peaked attention plausibly marks a
decoder already stalled, which this design cannot separate from a cause. Qwen3-TTS fuses text and
acoustic embeddings per position and cannot be checked at all.
